claim: Fear over side-effects is one of the main drivers of COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy.
source: Fear over side-effects is one of the main drivers of COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing literature on vaccine hesitancy, as indicated in the abstract and introduction sections.

claim: How risks are framed and presented to individuals affects their judgments of its severity.
source: A large literature in the behavioral and communication sciences finds that how risks are framed and presented to individuals affects their judgments of its severity.
evidence: This claim references a large body of literature in behavioral and communication sciences.

claim: Adding a descriptive risk label ('very low risk') next to the numerical side-effect increased participants' willingness to take the COVID-19 vaccine by 3.0 percentage points (p=0.003).
source: Adding a descriptive risk label ('very low risk') next to the numerical side-effect and providing a comparison to motor-vehicle mortality increased participants' willingness to take the COVID-19 vaccine by 3.0 percentage points (p=0.003)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the randomized controlled trial with statistical significance reported.

claim: Providing a comparison to motor-vehicle mortality increased participants' willingness to take the COVID-19 vaccine by 2.4 percentage points (p=0.049).
source: Adding a descriptive risk label ('very low risk') next to the numerical side-effect and providing a comparison to motor-vehicle mortality increased participants' willingness to take the COVID-19 vaccine by 3.0 percentage points (p=0.003) and 2.4 percentage points (p=0.049), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the randomized controlled trial with statistical significance reported.

claim: The effects of adding a risk label and motor-vehicle mortality comparison are independent and additive.
source: These effects were independent and additive and combining both framing strategies increased willingness to receive the vaccine by 6.1 percentage points (p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the combined effect equals approximately the sum of individual effects.

claim: Combining both framing strategies (risk label and motor-vehicle mortality comparison) increased willingness to receive the vaccine by 6.1 percentage points (p<0.001).
source: These effects were independent and additive and combining both framing strategies increased willingness to receive the vaccine by 6.1 percentage points (p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the randomized controlled trial with statistical significance reported.

claim: The framing effects operate by increasing individuals' perceptions of how safe the vaccine is.
source: Mechanistically, we find evidence that these framing effects operate by increasing individuals' perceptions of how safe the vaccine is.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on the secondary outcome measuring perceived vaccine safety.

claim: Low-cost side-effect framing strategies can meaningfully affect vaccine intentions at a population level.
source: Low-cost side-effect framing strategies can meaningfully affect vaccine intentions at a population level.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing statistically significant effects on vaccine intentions.

claim: The share of the US population that is fully vaccinated went from 2.4% in February 2021 to 34.5% in May 2021 but has since only risen to 63.9% in the following 9 months.
source: For example, in the United States, the share of the population that is fully vaccinated went from 2.4% in February 2021 to 34.5% in May 2021 but has since only risen to 63.9% in the following 9 months (Ritchie et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ritchie et al., 2022.

claim: The share of the UK population that is fully vaccinated was 71.3% as of February 9, 2022.
source: While not as stagnant, there is a similar pattern in the United Kingdom, where the share of the population that is fully vaccinated was just 71.3% as of February 9, 2022 (Ritchie et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ritchie et al., 2022.

claim: As of February 9, 2022, just 27.2% of adults in the United States have received a booster.
source: As of February 9, 2022, just 27.2% of adults in the United States and 55.1% of adults in the United Kingdom have received a booster
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to CDC and UK Health Security Agency data.

claim: As of February 9, 2022, 55.1% of adults in the United Kingdom have received a booster.
source: As of February 9, 2022, just 27.2% of adults in the United States and 55.1% of adults in the United Kingdom have received a booster
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to CDC and UK Health Security Agency data.

claim: Among those that received two doses, only 42.4% in the United States have received a third dose.
source: importantly, even among those that received two doses, only 42.4% in the United States and 77.3% in the United Kingdom have received a third (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021a; UK Health Security Agency, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to CDC and UK Health Security Agency data.

claim: Among those that received two doses, 77.3% in the United Kingdom have received a third dose.
source: importantly, even among those that received two doses, only 42.4% in the United States and 77.3% in the United Kingdom have received a third (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021a; UK Health Security Agency, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to CDC and UK Health Security Agency data.

claim: Fear and concern about vaccine side-effects is an important reason for vaccine hesitancy.
source: A common finding across these studies is that fear and concern about vaccine side-effects is an important reason for vaccine hesitancy.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to multiple studies on COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy.

claim: COVID-19 vaccine side-effects rates are extremely low (1 per 100,000 people vaccinated with AstraZeneca in the European Union).
source: Although COVID-19 vaccine side-effects rates are extremely low (1 per 100,000 people vaccinated with AstraZeneca in the European Union) (World Health Organization, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to WHO data.

claim: Side-effect rates were often presented by the media without context.
source: these rates were often presented by the media without context (Mueller and Eddy, 2021; Karp, 2021; Rivas, 2021; Saunt, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to media reports.

claim: Media presentation of side-effect rates without context likely led some individuals to reject vaccine uptake.
source: these rates were often presented by the media without context (Mueller and Eddy, 2021; Karp, 2021; Rivas, 2021; Saunt, 2021), likely leading some individuals to reject vaccine uptake (Pinna et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from media coverage patterns and citation to Pinna et al., 2021.

claim: The pausing of global COVID-19 vaccination efforts may have sent a strong signal that side-effects are a major cause of concern, thus increasing vaccine hesitancy.
source: In addition, the pausing of global COVID-19 vaccination efforts may have sent a strong signal that side-effects are a major cause of concern, thus increasing vaccine hesitancy.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the potential impact of vaccination pauses.

claim: Small financial incentives and reminders can improve COVID-19 and flu vaccine uptake.
source: Several recent behavioral sciences studies investigating this topic have found that small financial incentives and reminders can improve COVID-19 and flu vaccine uptake (Campos-Mercade et al., 2021; Milkman et al., 2021b; Milkman et al., 2021a; Dai et al., 2021; Klüver et al., 2021; Santos et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple behavioral science studies.

claim: Whether numerical risks are presented as percentages or natural frequencies can influence behavior.
source: For example, studies have shown that whether numerical risks are presented as percentages or natural frequencies (e.g. 1% compared to 1 out of 100), with a comparison to a commonly understood but different risk (e.g. the risk of motor-vehicle mortality), using infographics (e.g. visually showing the numbers of individuals in the numerator and denominator of a risk), with descriptive labels (e.g. putting 'very low risk' or 'high risk' next to the numerical risk) can all influence behavior.
evidence: This claim references existing studies on risk communication and framing effects.

claim: Individuals have a limited cognitive ability to process and internalize risk information, especially rare risks like COVID-19 side-effects.
source: Rather, research has shown that individuals have a limited cognitive ability to process and internalize risk information, especially rare risks like COVID-19 side-effects, and that individuals use mental guides or 'heuristics' to make sense of risk information that ultimately guides their decisions (Tversky and Kahneman, 1974; Gigerenzer and Gaissmaier, 2011; Trumbo, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational research on cognitive heuristics.

claim: Individuals use mental guides or 'heuristics' to make sense of risk information that ultimately guides their decisions.
source: Rather, research has shown that individuals have a limited cognitive ability to process and internalize risk information, especially rare risks like COVID-19 side-effects, and that individuals use mental guides or 'heuristics' to make sense of risk information that ultimately guides their decisions (Tversky and Kahneman, 1974; Gigerenzer and Gaissmaier, 2011; Trumbo, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational research on cognitive heuristics.

claim: Framing effects work by modifying the heuristics that individuals use to understand a risk in a way that does not strongly affect their incentives or remove their agency.
source: Therefore, framing effects work by modifying the heuristics that individuals use to understand a risk in a way that does not strongly affect their incentives or remove their agency.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited literature on heuristics and framing effects.

claim: The study conducted a randomized controlled trial among 8998 participants in the United States and the United Kingdom.
source: To answer these questions, we conducted a randomized controlled trial evaluating the effect of three framing strategies on COVID-19 vaccine intentions among 8988 adults ages 18+ (4502 adults in the United States and 4496 in the United Kingdom).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and sample size.

claim: The study examined three side-effect framing strategies: adding a qualitative risk label, adding a comparison group, and framing the comparison in relative rather than absolute terms.
source: We examined three side-effect framing strategies: what is the effect of adding a qualitative risk label next to the numerical risk, what is the effect of adding a comparison group (along with which comparison group is most effective), and for those with comparison groups, what is the effect of framing the comparison in relative rather than absolute terms (absolute comparisons of small risks may be cognitively harder for individuals to process than relative comparisons).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Two recent papers focused on COVID-19 have shown a strong link between individuals' COVID-19 vaccine intentions and their actual vaccination behavior.
source: While there is concern that vaccine intentions may not represent actual behavior, two recent papers focused on COVID-19 have shown a strong link between individuals' COVID-19 vaccine intentions and their actual vaccination behavior (Campos-Mercade et al., 2021; Klüver et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two specific studies.

claim: The study received ethical approval from the Medical Faculty of Heidelberg University Ethics Committee (#S-443/2021).
source: Prior to recruiting any participants, we received ethical approval for the study from the Medical Faculty of Heidelberg University Ethics Committee (#S-443/2021)
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: The trial was registered on the German Clinical Trials Registry (#DRKS00025551).
source: registered the trial, including the outcomes and treatments, on the German Clinical Trials Registry (#DRKS00025551)
evidence: This is a direct statement about trial registration.

claim: A trial protocol with a pre-analysis plan was published.
source: and published a trial protocol with a pre-analysis plan (Sudharsanan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the pre-analysis plan with citation.

claim: All participants provided informed consent through the Prolific platform.
source: All participants provided informed consent through the Prolific platform, including consent to publish.
evidence: This is a direct statement about informed consent procedures.

claim: The study used Prolific, an online-based service for recruiting participants for online-based research studies.
source: We used Prolific (Prolific, 2022), an online-based service for recruiting participants for online-based research studies to recruit the study participants.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the recruitment method.

claim: Participants were paid £0.63/$0.88 for the expected 5 min completion time.
source: Prolific participants are paid for their participation (we paid each participant £0.63/$0.88 for the expected 5 min completion time).
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant compensation.

claim: A stratified quota sampling procedure was used to match the education distribution of the sample to the general population.
source: Within Prolific, we used a stratified quota sampling procedure to match the education distribution of our sample to the general population (stratified by sex and country) based on available data for each country (Bureau U.S. Census, 2019; OECD, 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sampling methodology.

claim: The sample size was chosen to enable detection of a 5 percentage point difference between experimental arms with 80% power, a 5% alpha value, and a control proportion of 50%.
source: We chose this sample size to enable us to detect a 5 percentage point difference between the experimental arms with 80% power, a 5% alpha value, and a control proportion of 50%
evidence: This is a direct statement about the power calculation for sample size determination.

claim: 99% of participants were recruited between July 30, 2021, and August 10, 2021.
source: 99% of our participants were recruited between July 30, 2021, and August 10, 2021.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the recruitment timeline.

claim: The final 1% of participants were recruited between August 11, 2021, and October 4, 2021.
source: To reach our target quotas by sex and education, the final 1% of participants were recruited between August 11, 2021, and October 4, 2021.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the recruitment timeline.

claim: The study used a factorial randomization design to assign participants to three main factors.
source: We used a factorial randomization design to assign participants to three main factors (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the randomization design, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Factor 1 was whether there was a qualitative risk label saying 'very low risk' next to the numerical risk or not.
source: Factor 1 was whether there was a qualitative risk label saying 'very low risk' next to the numerical risk or not.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Factor 2 was whether the risk was presented with no comparison, a comparison to motor-vehicle mortality, or a comparison to COVID-19 mortality.
source: Factor 2 was whether the risk was presented with no comparison, a comparison to motor-vehicle mortality, or a comparison to COVID-19 mortality.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Factor 3 varied whether the comparison was presented in an absolute or relative way, only among those that received a comparison risk.
source: Factor 3 was only among that received a comparison risk and varied whether the comparison was presented in an absolute or relative way.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Participants were randomized to each factor independently, stratified by country.
source: We randomized participants to each factor independently (stratified by country)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the randomization procedure.

claim: The main outcome was a binary variable for whether participants reported 'yes' to the question of 'Would you take this vaccine if it were made available to you?'
source: Our main outcome was a binary variable for whether participants reported 'yes' to the question of 'Would you take this vaccine if it were made available to you?'
evidence: This is a direct statement about the primary outcome measure.

claim: The secondary outcome was participants' perception of how safe the vaccine is, based on a scale of 1 (extremely unsafe) to 10 (extremely safe).
source: Our secondary outcome was participants' perception of how safe the vaccine is, based on a scale of 1 (extremely unsafe) to 10 (extremely safe).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the secondary outcome measure.

claim: Four individuals from the UK sample did not complete the experiments and were excluded due to missing data (0.04%).
source: Four individuals from the UK sample did not complete the experiments and were therefore excluded due to missing data (0.04%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about missing data.

claim: The final sample consisted of 8998 individuals (99.96% response rate).
source: This resulted in a final sample of 8998 individuals (99.96% response rate).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the final sample size and response rate.

claim: In the US sample, 68.6% were between ages 18 and 30.
source: In the US and UK samples, 68.6% and 41.4% were between ages 18 and 30
evidence: This is descriptive data from Table 1 about the sample composition.

claim: In the UK sample, 41.4% were between ages 18 and 30.
source: In the US and UK samples, 68.6% and 41.4% were between ages 18 and 30
evidence: This is descriptive data from Table 1 about the sample composition.

claim: Among the control group, intentions to vaccinate were 65%.
source: As discussed in the following section, among our control group, intentions to vaccinate were 65%, which is closely aligned with the actual vaccination rate in the United States and United Kingdom at the time our data were being collected (Ritchie et al., 2022).
evidence: This is descriptive data about the control group baseline.

claim: Control group vaccine intentions (65%) were closely aligned with the actual vaccination rate in the United States and United Kingdom at the time data were being collected.
source: As discussed in the following section, among our control group, intentions to vaccinate were 65%, which is closely aligned with the actual vaccination rate in the United States and United Kingdom at the time our data were being collected (Ritchie et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim compares study data to real-world vaccination rates with citation.

claim: There is no evidence of imbalances in sociodemographic characteristics across the experimental groups.
source: We also find no evidence of imbalances in sociodemographic characteristics across the experimental groups (Tables 2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by balance tables showing no significant differences across groups.

claim: Adding a comparison to COVID-19 mortality had no evidence of an effect on vaccine intentions (effect size: 0.8 percentage points; 95% CI: –1.6, 3.2; p=0.496).
source: but no evidence of an effect of adding a comparison to COVID-19 mortality (effect size: 0.8 percentage points; 95% CI: –1.6, 3.2; p=0.496; control group mean: 65%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no statistically significant effect.

claim: There was no evidence that relative, compared to absolute, framings of comparisons had a large impact on willingness to take the hypothetical future COVID-19 vaccine (effect size: 1.3 percentage points; 95% CI: –1.1, 3.6; p=0.285).
source: Lastly, going against our expectation, we did not find evidence that relative, compared to absolute, framings of comparisons had a large impact on willingness to take the hypothetical future COVID-19 vaccine (effect size: 1.3 percentage points; 95% CI: –1.1, 3.6; p=0.285; control group mean: 67%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no statistically significant effect.

claim: The pattern of the framing effects on perceptions of vaccine safety closely mirrors the primary effects on willingness to take the vaccine.
source: Although the magnitude of the effect sizes is small, we find that the pattern of the framing effects on perceptions of vaccine safety closely mirrors the primary effects on willingness to take the vaccine.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of results for the two outcomes measured in the study.

claim: Perceptions of safety are one of the pathways through which these framing effects operate.
source: This suggests that perceptions of safety are indeed one of the pathways through which these framing effects operate, although our analyses do not exclude the possibility that by providing more information, these framing strategies also affect vaccine intentions by increasing the perceived trustworthiness or reliability of the information.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the pattern of results on the secondary outcome.

claim: Compared to those that received neither a quality risk label nor a comparison risk, those that received both strategies were 6.1 percentage points (95% CI: 2.8, 9.5; p<0.001) more likely to state that they would take the vaccine.
source: Compared to those that received neither a quality risk label nor a comparison risk (N=1499; control mean: 63%), those that received both strategies were 6.1 percentage points (95% CI: 2.8, 9.5; p<0.001) more likely to state that they would take the vaccine.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a non-pre-registered analysis.

claim: The effects of risk labeling and motor-vehicle mortality comparison are at a minimum independent and additive, with some indication that they may even be synergistic.
source: We find that at a minimum, the effects are independent and additive, with some indication that they may even be synergistic.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing the combined effect to the sum of individual effects.

claim: There is no evidence that the framing strategies vary across country, age, or sex.
source: We do not find evidence that the framing strategies vary across country, age, or sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by interaction analyses showing no significant differences.

claim: The results are consistent when using linear probability rather than logistic regression models.
source: Our results are consistent when we use linear probability rather than logistic regression models (Appendix 1—table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by robustness checks using alternative statistical models.

claim: The results are consistent when examining the outcome as a four-category ordinal (rather than binary) variable.
source: when we examine the outcome as a four-category ordinal (rather than binary) variable (Appendix 1—table 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by robustness checks using alternative outcome specifications.

claim: The results are consistent after excluding demographic control variables in the main regression analyses.
source: and after excluding demographic control variables in the main regression analyses (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by robustness checks using alternative model specifications.

claim: Even small changes in vaccination rates can have large health consequences at the population level.
source: This is an important and meaningful effect at the population level, where even small changes in vaccination rates can have large health consequences (Scobie et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Scobie et al., 2021.

claim: Motor-vehicle mortality may be a more salient heuristic against which individuals evaluate other risks than COVID-19 mortality.
source: One potential explanation for this finding is that at the time of our study, COVID-19 mortality was still a relatively new risk whereas individuals are generally familiar with motor-vehicle mortality. Thus, motor-vehicle mortality may be a more salient heuristic against which individuals evaluate other risks.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain an unexpected finding.

claim: Comparisons to commonly understood forms of mortality may produce greater behavioral changes than comparisons to novel or less common risks.
source: While speculative, this may suggest that comparisons to commonly understood forms of mortality may produce greater behavioral changes than comparisons to novel or less common risks.
evidence: This is explicitly labeled as speculative reasoning.

claim: Prior empirical work generally finds that relative risk framings produce a greater impact on behavior.
source: This is in contrast to prior empirical work which generally finds that relative risk framings produce a greater impact on behavior (Zipkin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zipkin et al., 2014.

claim: Campos-Mercade et al. find that among Swedish adults, paying individuals 24 USD increased vaccination rates by 4.2 percentage points.
source: Campos-Mercade et al. find that among Swedish adults, paying individuals 24 USD increased vaccination rates by 4.2 percentage points but found no evidence of impact from nudges that tried to influence behavior through social network effects and health information (Campos-Mercade et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Campos-Mercade et al., 2021.

claim: Campos-Mercade et al. found no evidence of impact from nudges that tried to influence behavior through social network effects and health information.
source: Campos-Mercade et al. find that among Swedish adults, paying individuals 24 USD increased vaccination rates by 4.2 percentage points but found no evidence of impact from nudges that tried to influence behavior through social network effects and health information (Campos-Mercade et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Campos-Mercade et al., 2021.

claim: Klüver et al. find evidence of moderate effects (between 2.2 and 3 percentage points) on vaccine intentions from larger payments (50 euros), providing freedoms to vaccinated individuals, and from allowing vaccination at local doctors.
source: Klüver et al. also study financial incentives and find a weaker effect among German adults when incentives were 25 euros, but evidence of moderate effects (between 2.2 and 3 percentage points) on vaccine intentions from larger payments (50 euros), providing freedoms to vaccinated individuals, and from allowing vaccination at local doctors (Klüver et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Klüver et al., 2021.

claim: Dai et al. find that text-messaged-based reminders with content based around different behavioral theories increased vaccination rates by 3.57 percentage points.
source: Dai et al. conduct a trial among adults enrolled in the UCLA health system and find that text-messaged-based reminders with content based around different behavioral theories increased vaccination rates by 3.57 percentage points (Dai et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dai et al., 2021.

claim: Santos et al. find that emails that emphasize social norms and reframe COVID-19 risks increased appointments for vaccination by around 3.5 percentage points.
source: Santos et al. study email-delivered nudges to patients in a large Pennsylvania health system and find that emails that emphasize social norms and similar to one of our main framings, those that reframe COVID-19 risks, increased appointments for vaccination by around 3.5 percentage points (Santos et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Santos et al., 2021.

claim: Moehring et al. find that providing individuals information about the share of their network that is accepting of vaccines influences individuals' own vaccination intentions.
source: Similarly, a multicountry randomized experiment by Moehring et al. finds that providing individuals information about the share of their network that is accepting of vaccines influences individuals' own vaccination intentions (Moehring et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moehring et al., 2000.

claim: Milkman et al. find that text-message-based nudges leveraging loss-aversion and social pressure can increase flu vaccination by up to 5 percentage points.
source: While not focused on COVID-19 vaccination, two recent studies by Milkman et al. find that text-message-based nudges leveraging loss-aversion and social pressure can increase flu vaccination by up to 5 percentage points (Milkman et al., 2021b; Milkman et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Milkman et al., 2021a and 2021b.

claim: Using self-reported intention to take the vaccine is potentially an important limitation if vaccine intentions do not translate into actual vaccine behavior.
source: Using self-reported intention to take the vaccine is potentially an important limitation if vaccine intentions do not translate into actual vaccine behavior.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: There is always a possibility that the effects observed here would be smaller or not present when measuring actual behavior.
source: However, there is always a possibility that the effects observed here would be smaller or not present when measuring actual behavior.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of uncertainty about generalization to actual behavior.

claim: The experiment deals with a hypothetical COVID-19 vaccine rather than one of the existing vaccines currently in use.
source: Relatedly, our experiment deals with a hypothetical COVID-19 vaccine rather than one of the existing vaccines currently in use.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The framing strategies presented may not apply to current vaccines if individuals' existing views hinder behavior change.
source: While we made this decision to guard against participant bias toward existing vaccines, the framing strategies we present here may not apply to current vaccines if individuals' existing views hinder behavior change.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a potential limitation.

claim: The study was not able to distinguish between those that had already been vaccinated and those that were yet to take any vaccine.
source: We were not able to distinguish between those that had already been vaccinated – either with one or two doses – and those that were yet to take any vaccine.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: The low rates of boosting among those who already received two doses in the United States is 41.7%.
source: The low rates of boosting among those who already received two doses in the United States (41.7%, Boas et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boas et al., 2020.

claim: The rate of boosting among those who already received two doses in the United Kingdom is 77.1%.
source: and the less than ideal rate in the United Kingdom (77.1%, UK Health Security Agency, 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to UK Health Security Agency, 2022.

claim: Just because individuals took two doses, they are not guaranteed to make the decision to take subsequent recommended doses.
source: reveal that just because individuals took two doses, they are not guaranteed to make the decision to take subsequent recommended doses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the booster uptake data.

claim: The use of an online-recruited sample has the potential to generate selection bias.
source: Our use of an online-recruited sample has the potential to generate selection bias in two important ways.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a potential limitation.

claim: The sample had a slight over-representation of younger adults, Asian Americans, and White Americans and a slight under-representation of older adults, Black Americans, and Hispanic Americans relative to the general US and UK adult populations.
source: However, relative to the general US and UK adult populations, our sample had a slight over-representation of younger adults, Asian Americans, and White Americans and a slight under-representation of older adults, Black Americans, and Hispanic Americans.
evidence: This is a direct statement about sample representativeness based on comparison to population data.

claim: A lack of representativity would only change the findings if those included in the study have a substantially different response to the framings than those that were not included.
source: Since our goal was not to generate a representative descriptive estimate but rather to estimate the effect of different framings, a lack of representativity would only change our findings if those included in the study have a substantially different response to the framings than those that were not included.
evidence: This is reasoning about the implications of non-representativeness for causal inference.

claim: Prolific attempts to reduce selection bias by randomly selecting a subset of eligible participants and sending them invitations to participate every 48 hr until the sample size is reached.
source: Prolific attempts to reduce this bias by randomly selecting a subset of eligible participants and sending them invitations to participate every 48 hr until the sample size is reached.
evidence: This is a direct statement about Prolific's recruitment procedures.

claim: It is unlikely that selection bias from self-selection into the study will have affected the results as randomization uniformly distributes topic-specific selection bias across the trial arms.
source: Regardless, it is unlikely that this type of selection bias will have affected our results as randomization uniformly distributes topic-specific selection bias across the trial arms.
evidence: This is reasoning about how randomization addresses selection bias concerns.

claim: Despite increasingly strong vaccination hesitancy and exposure to large amounts of vaccine information, low-cost side-effect framing strategies can meaningfully affect vaccination intentions at a population level.
source: Our results reveal that despite increasingly strong vaccination hesitancy and exposure to large amounts of vaccine information, low-cost side-effect framing strategies can meaningfully affect vaccination intentions at a population level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Vaccination for COVID-19 will likely remain an important priority for the foreseeable future.
source: Given that vaccination for COVID-19 will likely remain an important priority for the foreseeable future, these insights can be valuable for increasing the uptake of future vaccination efforts.
evidence: This is a statement about the ongoing importance of COVID-19 vaccination based on general knowledge.

claim: The insights from this study can be valuable for increasing the uptake of future vaccination efforts.
source: Given that vaccination for COVID-19 will likely remain an important priority for the foreseeable future, these insights can be valuable for increasing the uptake of future vaccination efforts.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the practical implications of the study findings.

claim: Of the 9002 enrolled participants, 8998 individuals completed the survey (response rate = 99.96%).
source: Of the 9002 enrolled participants, 8998 individuals completed the survey (response rate = 99.96%).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the United States, motor-vehicle mortality in 2020 was 12 per 100,000 population.
source: In the United States, for example, motor-vehicle mortality in 2020 was 12 per 100,000 population
evidence: This is a factual statement about mortality rates, though no citation is provided in the extracted text.

claim: In the United States, COVID-19 mortality in 2020 was 170 per 100,000 population.
source: while COVID-19 mortality in the same year was 170 per 100,000 population.
evidence: This is a factual statement about mortality rates, though no citation is provided in the extracted text.

claim: The study chose a side-effect rate that was comparable to the current vaccines.
source: We presented participants with information on a hypothetical future COVID-19 vaccine including information on its side-effect rate (we focused on the risk of serious blood clots and chose a side-effect rate that was comparable to the current vaccines) (European Medicines Agency (EMA), 2021; U.S. Food and Drug, 2021).
